# MTP draft cost and a reduced draft vocabulary (block 17c, 2026-09-24)

Question: what does drafting cost per speculative cycle, and does a draft head limited
to the first N token ids (`--spec-draft-vocab N`) make speculative decoding faster
without changing outputs? [Spec](../specs/speculative.md) ("Draft vocabulary").

## Setup

- RX 7900 XTX, Mesa 26.2.3 RADV; Qwen3.8-27B Q4_0 (model sha256 prefix
  `ede16c7b36e578ca`); zerv built from `3c03b07` plus the uncommitted working tree
  (server sha256 prefix `40f08ad12cf4ec69`, `zig build server -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
  -Dcpu=native`).
- Draft cost: `zerv-mtp-check MODEL TOKENS OUTDIR [N]` (new timing section: wall-clock
  `draft(t, k)` with 1 pending row after a step and 3 after a 3-row commit, k = 1..4,
  median of 41 after 8 warm-up calls; the fixtures `third_party/mtp-check/tokens-{short-nothink,long-think}.json`).
  Raw data: [mtp-check/](data/2026-09-24-draft-vocab/mtp-check/).
- Serving: `bench/run_serving.py`, 3 drafts with the adaptive policy, 2 repeats,
  greedy, 512 tokens:
  - `--workload bench/workloads/decode-v1.json --output docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-draft-vocab/decode-v1`
  - `--workload bench/workloads/decode-multilingual-v1.json --output docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-draft-vocab/multilingual-v1`
    (new workload: five languages, long answers in the prompt's language)
  - engines `"zerv;zerv-spec3;zerv-spec3@spec-draft-vocab=131072;zerv-spec3@spec-draft-vocab=65536;zerv-spec3@spec-draft-vocab=32768"`.

## Draft cost

A draft pass reads the MTP layer (253 MiB) and the Q6_K output head (995 MiB):
1.31 GB, 1.42 ms at 920 GB/s. The head alone is 80% of the bytes and already runs at
916 GB/s ([decode baseline](2026-09-24-decode-baseline.md)).

| draft(t, k), ms (short-nothink, 1 pending row) | k = 1 | k = 2 | k = 3 | k = 4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| full vocabulary (248,320) | 1.601 | 3.140 | 4.656 | 6.178 |
| N = 131,072 | 1.053 | 2.036 | 3.028 | 4.022 |
| N = 65,536 | 0.741 | 1.406 | 2.085 | 2.758 |
| N = 32,768 | 0.584 | 1.099 | 1.625 | 2.150 |

The long-think fixture and 3 pending rows are within 0.1 ms of these values (raw data).
With full drafts, 3 drafts cost 4.66 ms per cycle against 25.0 ms for the 4-row
verify + commit, so **drafting is 16% of a 3-draft cycle**.

## Correctness (gate 1)

- Full vocabulary with this build: all 18 dump files byte-identical to earlier runs on
  both fixtures (`timing-short`, `2026-09-24-fma-long-think`, `2026-09-24-final-long-think`).
- N = 131,072, 65,536 and 32,768 on both fixtures: every draft-logits dump equals the
  first N values of the full run bitwise (for each chain step whose inputs match the
  full run), and every draft is the first argmax of its dumped prefix. Scenario C
  (steps ≡ draft/verify/commit) 3/3 in every run. One divergence, as specified: at
  N = 32,768 the full head's draft 36093 is out of range and the reduced head drafts
  3299; the chain after it differs.

## Serving: decode-v1 (English, code, JSON, reasoning)

Decode tok/s, median of 2; accepted/verified drafts of repeat 0. All outputs are
byte-identical to plain decode (`zerv`, 50.7–50.8 tok/s).

| engine | code | json | think | prose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 drafts, full (default) | 120.6 (369/423) | 124.9 (374/407) | 107.7 (351/463) | 75.6 (278/615) |
| N = 131,072 | 127.6 (369/423) | 132.3 (374/407) | 113.8 (350/461) | 80.2 (277/607) |
| N = 65,536 | **131.9** (369/425) | **134.1** (371/414) | 117.8 (350/461) | **82.6** (275/603) |
| N = 32,768 | 129.8 (364/431) | 125.9 (359/443) | **118.2** (347/450) | 81.4 (262/571) |

N = 65,536: +7 to +9% with acceptance nearly unchanged.

## Serving: multilingual (negative result)

| engine | chinese | japanese | russian | german | korean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plain decode | 50.6 | 50.6 | 50.6 | 50.6 | 50.6 |
| 3 drafts, full (default) | **74.3** (268/549) | **73.1** (264/553) | **75.2** (272/528) | **87.5** (310/515) | **69.8** (253/586) |
| N = 131,072 | 75.8 (258/537) | 68.0 (225/570) | 61.4 (187/525) | 85.3 (286/482) | 61.0 (191/531) |
| N = 65,536 | 49.6 (89/319) | 58.6 (160/397) | 60.4 (169/376) | 84.4 (273/401) | 60.9 (171/400) |
| N = 32,768 | 51.7 (88/338) | 59.6 (146/348) | 59.0 (145/364) | 80.6 (249/381) | 58.1 (142/392) |

All outputs byte-identical to plain decode. Share of generated tokens at ids ≥ N
(llama-tokenize on the plain-decode outputs):

| language | ≥ 32,768 | ≥ 65,536 | ≥ 131,072 | ≥ 151,643 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| chinese | 82.2% | 82.2% | 6.2% | 0.0% |
| japanese | 65.4% | 61.1% | 26.2% | 23.6% |
| russian | 64.8% | 56.1% | 52.0% | 37.1% |
| german | 29.2% | 17.4% | 12.9% | 12.9% |
| korean | 64.3% | 51.0% | 44.7% | 34.2% |

For English, code and JSON the same shares are 0.2–3.7% at ≥ 65,536 (decode-v1
outputs; the 75.5k-token long-v2 prompt: 2.2%).

## Interpretation

- Output is unaffected in every run, as designed: verification decides.
- Id order is a good frequency proxy only for English-like text. The Chinese pieces sit
  at ids 65,536–131,071 and much of the Cyrillic, Korean and Japanese vocabulary lies
  above 131,072. A prefix head cannot draft those tokens, and acceptance collapses:
  Chinese at N = 65,536 falls below plain decode.
- Decision: **the knob stays opt-in** (`--spec-draft-vocab full` by default, the
  previous behavior). N = 65,536 is the measured best for English and code deployments
  (+7–9% on decode-v1); for other languages it is slower.
- Follow-up: a frequency-ranked subset (row indirection in the head matvec plus an
  index → id map in the argmax) could keep the gain across languages. It needs a
  representative token-frequency source; the ranking must not be fit to the benchmark
  outputs.

# Explicit f16 prefill mode (block 14): speed, accuracy and the matched comparison

Date: 2026-09-24. Question: can zerv match llama-server's fast prompt path at the same
arithmetic class (the same GGUF, f16 WMMA), while staying at least as accurate?
[Spec](specs/prefill.md#explicit-f16-prefill-mode--block-14-specified-2026-09-24-before-implementation);
the background is in [llama precision](2026-09-23-llama-precision.md).

**Result.**

- **Speed:** on par or better at 23, 81 and 836 prompt tokens, and within 4% at 3223.
- **Quality:** more accurate than llama's matched config (nof16) in the mean,
  median, p90 and p99, and far more accurate than llama's default. Gate 2 as
  declared ("worst token ≤ llama nof16's") is **not met**: the single worst token
  is 20% worse on one case.
- **Status:** FP32 remains the default; f16 is opt-in (`--prefill-precision f16`).
  Block 14 stays open.

## What was built

- **`src/model/gemm_f16.comp`**: f16×f16→f32 WMMA with a 128×128 tile and 4 wave64
  subgroups of 64×64.
  - Q4_0, Q4_1 and Q5_K weights are dequantized exactly in f32 and rounded once to
    f16; X is rounded once to f16.
  - Accumulation is WMMA f32, one 16-k slice per step in k order. This is the same
    class as llama's `matmul_quant_f16` with f32 accumulation.
- **Scope** (`gemm.f16Eligible`): quantized projections with M ≥ 4096 and
  M % 128 == 0, in 128/256/512-row plans. Everything else stays FP32: attn_k/v,
  ssm_alpha/beta, attention, DeltaNet, norms, the KV cache, the output head and all
  of decode.
- **Interfaces:**
  - `Options.prefill_precision`, `--prefill-precision fp32|f16` (server, profile
    and capture tools), `verify_model.py --precision`;
  - `Device.open(.cooperative_matrix)` now also enables `VK_KHR_vulkan_memory_model`,
    which the coopmat shaders declare (bindings regenerated: 51 structs, 72 constants);
  - `init` fails with `UnsupportedDevice` without coopmat or wave64. There is no
    silent fallback.
- **Kernel choice.** It comes from a prototype sweep
  ([sweep-r1.jsonl](bench/data/2026-09-24-wmma-gemm/sweep-r1.jsonl),
  [source](bench/data/2026-09-24-wmma-gemm/experiments/gemm_wmma.comp); ffn_gate at
  512 rows):
  - An exact-integer-weight variant with per-block f32 scaling peaked at
    49.2 TFLOP/s, with normalized error 2.1e-4 against FP32.
  - Rounding the weights to f16 (llama's arithmetic) reached 59.5 TFLOP/s, with
    2.7e-4.
  - Per shape: 54–62 TFLOP/s against llama default's 47–59 (GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER,
    [logs](bench/data/2026-09-24-wmma-gemm/)). attn_k (M=1024) reached only

Specs: [prefill.md, "Fused prefill attention"](../specs/prefill.md),
[speculative

[kv-buffers](2026-09-24-kv-buffers.md). Every GPU run was checked for a concurrent

## 1. Fused prefill attention (`src/model/flash.comp`)

Before, attention materialized 24 × chunk × context FP32 scores: score GEMM, row softmax,
P·V GEMM. It ran at about 10 TFLOP/s, and the region grew with context (1.8 GB at
512 × 38,400).

**Kernel (v2, shipped).** One workgroup per KV head and 8 query rows. Six 64-thread groups
handle the 6 query heads that share the KV head, so the caches serve their identical K/V
reads.
- Scores over a 128-key tile: lane l owns keys 2l and 2l + 1. Q is wave-uniform (scalar
  loads) and K is read directly, one 4-dim step ahead.
- Row max and sum use subgroup reductions; the online softmax keeps m, l and O.
- P goes to LDS; each lane accumulates 4 head dims of the 8 rows (V read directly, 4 keys
  ahead).
- Accuracy structure: 32-dim partial sums per score and a per-tile output partial
  (O = O·a + O_tile).

**Development path** (per-phase GPU time of an 8,192-token fp32 prefill,
`zerv-model-profile MODEL 8704 512 8192 4 fp32`; single runs,
[raw](data/2026-09-24-flash/profiles/)):

| Variant | prefill GPU ms | attention ms | chunk at 0 | at 3584 | at 7680 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| materialized (before) | 14,275 | 2,030 | 11.9 | 124.7 | 237.7 |
| v1: 64 rows × 1 head, K/V staged in LDS, 4×4 micro-tiles | 13,644 | 1,480 | 11.3 | 87.8 | 172.7 |
| v2 (above) without prefetch | 14,076 | 1,867 | — | — | 223.7 |
| **v2 with prefetch** (RW 8, 6 heads, 4 keys per P·V step) | **12,978** | **722** | **4.4** | **42.4** | **86.5** |
| v2, RW 4 | 13,124 | 802 | 4.8 | 46.7 | 95.9 |
| v2, RW 12 | 13,176 | 939 | 6.4 | 55.4 | 110.4 |
| v2, RW 16, 3 heads (252 VGPRs) | 13,933 | 1,734 | 10.7 | 102.7 | 199.9 |
| v2, RW 16, 2 heads | 13,363 | 1,158 | 7.3 | 70.7 | 133.8 |
| v2, subgroup instead of workgroup barriers around P | 13,022 | 720 | 4.5 | 42.1 | 86.0 |
| v2, 8 keys per P·V step (252 VGPRs) | 13,167 | 918 | 5.4 | 53.9 | 108.8 |

- Attention is 2.8× faster over an 8k prompt (2,030 → 720 ms), about 18.6 TFLOP/s at the
  7680 chunk against about 6.7 before.
- v1 lost to LDS bandwidth: two 16-byte LDS reads per 16 FMAs.
- v1 was also less accurate: one 256-term dot-product chain and one output chain over
  all keys. `attn_pregate` mean normalized L2 error was 1.0e-6 against 4.8e-7
  materialized; `attn_output` reached 0.956 of its bound in the chunked modes. Partial
  sums fixed that (component worst error 2.2e-3 → 6.8e-4 of the bound).

**Gates (all executed):**
- **Component:** `tests/model_gpu.zig`, the FP64 first-order bound. Covers row blocks,
  tile edges, a context not a multiple of 64, NaN past the live keys and past the
  count, and untouched outputs. Worst error is 7.8e-4 of the bound; 26/26 GPU tests.
- **Model:** `tools/verify_model.py`, default oracles modes 0/1/13/512/512:17 and long
  oracle modes 0/13/128/512/512:300; all pass. The worst per-case tensor is at
  0.25–0.75 of its bound (the materialized path had 0.72 on the long oracle).
  Reports: [default](data/2026-09-24-flash/verify-final-default.json),
  [long](data/2026-09-24-flash/verify-final-long.json).
- **Decode unchanged:** mode-0 logits and captures are bitwise identical to the
  pre-change build on all three oracle cases.

**Materialized path removed.** It had no remaining advantage. Removed: the option, the
softmax kernel, the attention GEMM kernels and the prefill score matrix. The other
model modules are byte-identical. The score region keeps decode's 24 × decode rows ×
context.

**Process failure found and fixed before any release.** The first build sized the score
region to zero, but decode and verify write their scores there. They then wrote into
the split-K partials, which was harmless at 512-row chunks but not guaranteed for small
plans. Details are in `TODO.md`. Fixed, with a layout test, an init check and mode 0 in
the gate.

## 2. Batched MTP catch-up

The MTP KV depends only on u = `eh_proj([enorm(embed x); hnorm(h)])`, `attn_norm`, K, V,
and the k-norm and RoPE. The ≤ 5-row catch-up passes computed the whole layer at about
0.33 ms per prompt token.

It now runs inside the prefill command:
- the embeddings into `cat` (row stride 2H), then `copy2d` of the shifted h rows beside
  them;
- in-place enorm and hnorm;
- `eh_proj` on a new Q8_0 GEMM (`gemm.comp` FORMAT 8, exact d·q);
- `attn_norm`, K and V GEMMs, `qk_b` into KV cache 16;
- `hp` ← the last row.

**Gates:**
- The Q8_0 GEMM against FP64 (wide tile = narrow tile bitwise, split-K, untouched dead
  rows).
- The MTP FP64 gate: h' and logits within 2–5e-7, every draft the FP64 argmax
  ([data](data/2026-09-24-mtp-gate/)).
- `zerv-spec-check` 11/11.

TTFT, serving-v2 and long-v1 (the f16 speculative outputs byte-identical to the
non-speculative ones):

| Prompt | f16, 3 drafts, before | after | f16, no speculation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 836 tokens | 1,096 ms | 968 ms | 961 ms |
| 3,223 tokens | 3,574 ms | 3,081 ms | 3,072 ms |
| 37,827 tokens | 82.2 s | 70.0 s (46.2 s with fused attention) | 70.0 s (46.0 s) |

([serving-v2 before](data/2026-09-24-speculative/serving-v2/),
[after](data/2026-09-24-speculative/serving-v2-catchup/)).

## 3. Sampling

Sampled decode ran at 46 tok/s against 48 greedy. The sampler copied all 248,320 logits
into candidate structs and quickselected them for every token, about 0.9 ms.

`top_k` (≤ 256, which includes the model defaults) now takes one vectorized pass with a
running k-th-best threshold. Penalized ids are inserted afterwards with their penalized
logit. The order (logit, then id) is total, so the kept set is identical, and so is the
rest of the chain.

Gate: draw-for-draw equality with the old full-array path (`fast_top_k = false`) over
12 × 60 draws on 50k-token vocabularies with ties and positive and negative penalties.
Greedy argmax is vectorized too. Speed measurement follows in the next serving run.

## 3b. Wave32 (negative result, 2026-09-24 later)

RDNA3 dual-issues FMAs (VOPD) only in wave32, and the kernel supports 32-wide subgroups
(cross-subgroup reductions through LDS). An experiment build created the flash pipeline
with a required subgroup size (`zerv-model-profile MODEL 8704 512 8192 4 fp32`, 2 runs
each, [data](data/2026-09-24-flash/wave32/)):

| Subgroup size | prefill GPU ms | attention ms | chunk at 7680 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| driver default (64) | 12,977 / 12,967 | 717 / 716 | 85.7 / 85.5 |
| required 32 | 13,180 / 13,132 | 939 / 936 | 112.0 / 111.1 |
| required 64 | 12,988 / 12,963 | 717 / 717 | 85.7 / 85.8 |

Wave32 is 31% slower; the experiment option was removed. Remaining levers for prefill
attention: cooperative-matrix (WMMA) attention in the f16 prefill mode (a precision
change, opt-in), recorded in `TODO.md`.

## 4. Long context against llama-server (37,827 tokens, cold, [raw](data/2026-09-24-flash/long-v1/))

`bench/run_serving.py --workload bench/workloads/long-v1.json --context 38400
--no-prompt-cache`, 2 repeats. All engines answered correctly.

| Engine | TTFT s | decode tok/s (23 tokens) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| zerv f16 | 46.0 / 46.0 | 36.2 |
| zerv f16, 3 drafts | 46.2 / 46.2 | 58.4 |
| zerv fp32 | 73.9 / 74.3 | 36.1 |
| llama-server default (FA, ub 512) | 46.6 / 46.6 | 36.4 / 37.3 |
| llama-server MTP 3 | 50.4 / 50.4 | 71.6 / 71.5 |

- Open at long context: llama's MTP decode is faster (71.5 against 58.4). zerv's verify

## 5. Verify attention grid order, long context (37,822–37,827 tokens, cold, [raw](data/2026-09-24-flash/long-v1-r2/))

Change: the verify pass's `attn_scores` and `attn_pv` grids are now (rows, chunks, KV
heads) rather than (chunks, KV heads, rows). The rows of one chunk now run next to each
other and share that chunk's K/V through L2, instead of each row streaming the whole
cache from DRAM. The arithmetic per output is unchanged. Gates: verify_model modes
0/1/13/512/512:17 bitwise equal to the previous captures, and `zerv-spec-check` 11/11.

# FMA accumulation in the decode and verify matvec (block 17c, 2026-09-24)

Question: the multi-row verify matvec is ALU-bound at 3–5 rows
([spec-verify](2026-09-24-spec-verify.md)); a fused multiply-add per step (one rounding
instead of two) was measured faster in the lab but rejected in 08c for changing output
bits. With the FP64 gates as the criterion, is it correct, and is it faster?
[Spec](../specs/matvec-push.md) ("FMA accumulation").

## Change

`accum()` in `src/matvec/matvec.comp` and `matvec_rows.comp`:
`precise vec4 added=fma(w,x,sum)` instead of `precise` multiply then add. Decode of
weights, lane partition, block order, the two partial vectors and the reduction tree are
unchanged. Then the per-count verify table re-tuned (below).

## Correctness

| Gate | Result ([data](data/2026-09-24-fma-matvec/)) |
| --- | --- |
| `zig build gpu-test` | 29/29: all 48 matvec fixtures in both layouts (exact cases unchanged: products and sums there are representable), multi-row = single-row bitwise on all fixtures and real shapes |
| `verify_model`, default oracle, modes 0/1/13/512/512:17 | passed, 0 failures; decode-mode logits worst normalized L2 2.27e-6 → 2.01e-6 (short), 4.08e-6 → 1.56e-6 (long-think) |
| `verify_model`, long oracle, modes 0/13/128/512/512:300 | passed; mode 0 logits 2.05e-5 → 1.56e-5, worst/bound 0.639 → 0.448; prefill modes as before |
| `zerv-spec-check` (f32 and f16 KV) | 11/11 each, with the final table |
| `zerv-mtp-check` scenario C + FP64 MTP reference | 3/3 and passed on both sequences |
| `zerv-prefix-check` | gate passed |

One rounding per step makes decode more accurate against FP64 on every oracle case.

## Verify table re-tune

`python3 tools/tune_matvec_rows.py --output docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-fma-matvec/rows-tune`
(new tool: compiles each (GROUP, CB) variant of `matvec_rows.comp`, runs
`zerv-matvec-rows-bench` over 8 roles, 2 passes in alternating order). Two findings:

- **G = 4 at 5 rows is not bitwise equal to the single-row module for Q5_K (ssm_out)
  and Q6_K (output)**. It was never shipped; the tool now marks such variants invalid
  instead of stopping. Cause not investigated at the time; found later the same day: an
  ACO miscompile of VGPR spills in LDS ([RCA](2026-09-24-aco-lds-spill.md)).
- The sums from this tool drifted against the 17b.1 sweep by 30–56% on the mid-size
  roles, for the single-row passes too (e.g. `attn_q` single 1,053 → 1,640 µs at
  count 2), while the largest roles did not move. Separate processes are not
  comparable at that level (D6), so the decision was made by an interleaved in-model
  race instead.

Race: three `zerv-spec-check` binaries run A B C A B C A B C
([data](data/2026-09-24-fma-matvec/ab-race/), binary hashes in `binaries.sha256`):
A = multiply-add, old table {2: (2,2), 3: (2,2), 4: (3,2), 5: (2,4)}; B = FMA, old
table; C = FMA, the sweep's best {2: (3,2), 3: (3,3), 4: (3,2), 5: (3,3)}. Median of 3
(each is itself a median of 41 calls), ms:

| | A mul+add, old | B FMA, old | **C FMA, new** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| decode step | 20.16 | 20.13 | 20.14 |
| verify+commit 1 row | 20.70 | 20.73 | 20.71 |
| 2 rows | **21.51** | 21.64 | 21.58 |
| 3 rows | 24.24 | 26.03 | **22.68** |
| 4 rows | 27.30 | 24.95 | **25.03** |
| 5 rows | 32.60 | 30.59 | **28.77** |

Spread within each cell ≤ 0.2 ms except one 20.92 outlier (B, 1 row).

## Decision

- **Adopted: C.** 3 rows (the default: 3 drafts, adaptive) −6.4%, 4 rows −8.3%,
  5 rows −11.7% per verify; 2 rows +0.3%; single-row decode unchanged. `ROWS_CONFIG` in
  `tools/compile_matvec.py` and `matvec.rows_groups` = {1, 3, 3, 3, 3}.

## Knob (added the same day)

`--matvec-accumulation fma|separate` (default fma) keeps the previous arithmetic
selectable: `separate` compiles the modules with `ACCUM_FMA 0` and its old verify table.
Gates: gpu-test 30/30 (both module sets on every fixture, multi-row = single-row for
both), `verify_model --matvec-accumulation separate` byte-identical to the pre-FMA
captures (`2026-09-24-kvtype-f32-*`, 28 + 14 files), spec-check 11/11 in both modes
(step 19.67 / 19.79 ms, 3-row verify 22.53 / 24.11 ms).

Serving check through the flag (decode-v1, 3 drafts, 1 repeat, same server build;
`python3 bench/run_serving.py --workload bench/workloads/decode-v1.json --output
docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-fma-matvec/decode-v1-knob --engines
"zerv-spec3;zerv-spec3@matvec-accumulation=separate" --repeats 1`):

| decode tok/s | code | json | think | prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fma (default) | 121.0 | 125.4 | 107.7 | 75.6 |
| separate | 111.7 | 115.4 | 100.6 | 71.3 |

Greedy outputs are identical between the two modes on all four cases (`output_sha256`).
With one repeat this confirms that the flag works; it does not measure variance. The
speedup numbers remain the ones in the serving table below.

## Serving (decode-v1, greedy, 512 tokens, 2 repeats; [data](data/2026-09-24-fma-matvec/decode-v1/))

`bench/run_serving.py --workload bench/workloads/decode-v1.json --engines
zerv,zerv-spec2,zerv-spec3,llama-fa-ub512-mtp4 --repeats 2`. The binary also contains the
decode attention changes of [decode-attention-long](2026-09-24-decode-attention-long.md)
(neutral at these short contexts). Decode tok/s median [min–max]; acceptance =
accepted / verified drafts:

| zerv (no speculation) | 49.8 | 49.7 | 49.5 | 49.8 |
| zerv, 2 drafts | 108.2 (0.92) | 110.3 (0.95) | 102.0 (0.84) | **78.6** (0.53) |
| **zerv, 3 drafts (default)** | **120.5** (0.87) | **124.8** (0.92) | **107.7** (0.76) | 75.6 (0.45) |

| zerv 3 drafts before (decode-v1-adaptive) | 110.0 | 114.0 | 99.1 | 71.2 |

- 3 drafts are 9–10% faster than before on code, json and think; zerv is 1.15 / 1.14 /

# f16 WMMA prefill GEMM lab, round 1 (block 16b, 2026-09-24)

Question: how fast can the f16 WMMA prefill GEMM (`--prefill-precision f16`) get on the
RX 7900 XTX while staying **bitwise identical** to the shipped kernel
(`src/model/gemm_f16.comp`, already gated in block 14)? The plan and decision log are in
[design/speed.md](../design/speed.md).

## Method

- **Harness:** [bench/run_gemm_f16.py](../../bench/run_gemm_f16.py) runs `zerv-gemm-bench`
  (with its new `--warmup-ms`, `--wave` and `--x-f16` options) on the real model weights
  for every f16-eligible shape at 512 rows.
  - 8 s (baseline: 10 s) of sustained warm-up, then 200 timed samples; the median is
    reported.
  - A sampler thread records the shader clock and board power from sysfs.
  - With `--dump --reference-dump`, every result Y is compared **bytewise** against the
    shipped kernel's result in the same run.
- **Lab sources:**
  - [gemm_f16_ablate.comp](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/gemm_f16_ablate.comp): the
    shipped kernel plus `ABL_*` switches. With no switch it compiles to a module
    byte-identical to the shipped one for all three formats.
  - [gemm_f16_v2.comp](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/gemm_f16_v2.comp): a parametric
    kernel (wave size, tile, wave layout, `FASTDQ`, `LDS128`, `MANUAL_FRAG`, `XDIRECT`).
  - Built with the pinned glslc/spirv-val flags (`bench/gemm_lab/build.py`).
- **Invariant used as the gate.** Every variant keeps each output's sequence of 16-k WMMA
  steps in k order. Tile shape, buffering, wave layout and the data path therefore cannot
  change a single bit. A result that does not match is a bug.
- **Device:** power cap 339 W, `auto` performance level, Mesa 26.2.3 RADV.
- **Data:** [runs](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/runs/) (raw JSONL + manifests per
  run), [ISA dumps](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/isa/), [hashes](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/hashes.sha256).

## Findings, in order

1. **Baseline (shipped, 10 s warm-up):** 53–69 TFLOP/s.
   - The largest GEMMs run **at the 339 W power cap**, with clocks falling to 2.6–2.8 GHz.
   - Less data movement therefore also buys clock.
2. **Ablations of the shipped kernel** (1× = baseline):

   | Work removed | Speed-up |
   | --- | --- |
   | Fragment loads from LDS (`coopMatLoad`) | **1.8–2.0×** (106–129 TFLOP/s) |
   | Dequantization | 1.14–1.25× |
   | X load and convert | 1.06–1.11× |
   | Barriers | 1.04–1.13× |

3. **Why LDS fragment loads dominate** (ISA, [baseline](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/isa/baseline-q4_0.txt)):
   - RADV runs the kernel as wave64. A and B operands are 8 VGPRs (16 halves) per lane,
     and RDNA3 requires them replicated from lanes 0–15 to 16–31, and in wave64 also to
     32–63 (AMD GPUOpen, "How to accelerate AI applications on RDNA 3 using WMMA",
     read 2026-09-24).
   - So every lane loads 32 bytes per fragment: 4× the data in wave64.
   - RADV emits 4× `ds_load_b64` per fragment: 64 per 32 WMMAs.
4. **v2a (wave64, two LDS stages, register prefetch, one barrier per step):**
   bitwise-equal, but **slower** (46–57 TFLOP/s). Negative, retained.
5. **`RADV_PERFTEST=cswave32` does not apply to this shader.**
   - The dump still shows `min/max_subgroup_size: 64`.
   - The first "wave32" runs therefore ran half the waves and computed half of each
     tile. Their 82–104 "TFLOP/s" are **invalid**; the bitwise gate caught it (50% of
     outputs never written).
   - Fix: real subgroup size control. `VK_EXT_subgroup_size_control` was added to the
     bindings (three structs, generated and regenerated identically; the ABI fixture is
     now 56 structs / 77 constants), with `gpu.Device.Options.subgroup_size_control` and
     `gpu.Kernel.Options.subgroup_size`.
   - Verified in the ISA: `api/min/max_subgroup_size: 32`, v8 accumulators.
6. **Wave32 results** (all bitwise-equal to the shipped kernel, so wave32 and wave64
   WMMA accumulate identically):
   - w32a, 128×128 with 8 waves of 32×64: about equal to the baseline.
   - w32b, 256×128 with 8 waves of 64×64: 63–77 TFLOP/s.
   - **w32c, 128×256 with 8 waves of 64×64:** 65–79 TFLOP/s. Each weight is dequantized
     half as often per GEMM.
7. **FASTDQ (Q4_0):** nibbles are ORed into the f16 pattern `0x6400` (= 1024 + q,
   exact), then one packed subtract of 1032 and one packed multiply by the f16 scale.
   - Bitwise-equal, so f16 subnormals are preserved.
   - +1–3% on w32c; under −4% on w32b.
8. **Ablations of w32c + FASTDQ:** LDS fragment loads 1.46–1.61×, dequantization
   1.22–1.24× (mostly through power: clocks rise about 250 MHz), barriers 1.09–1.13×.
9. **LDS128 / MANUAL_FRAG** (16-byte typed LDS, explicit `uvec4` loads):
   - RADV's NIR still splits shared loads into 8 bytes (`load_shared ... align_mul=16`,
     emitted as `ds_load_b64`); stores stay 16 bytes.
   - No gain. Negative, retained.
   - But **MANUAL_FRAG is bitwise-equal**, which **verifies the RDNA3 fragment layout
     on real weights**: element i of lane l is k index i of row (A) or column (B)
     l % 16.
10. **XDIRECT** (w32c + FASTDQ + B fragments straight from f16 X in global memory: two
    `buffer_load_b128` per fragment, no LDS for B):
    - Half the `ds_load` instructions (32 per 32 WMMAs), 20 KB of LDS.
    - Bitwise-equal. **74–86 TFLOP/s, 1.23–1.28× the shipped kernel** on the Q4_0 shapes.

| Shape (512 rows) | Shipped | w32c | w32c + FASTDQ | **XDIRECT** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ffn_gate (Q4_0) | 67.8 | 77.6 | 78.5 | **84.1** |
| ffn_down (Q4_0) | 59.5 | 65.2 | 65.6 | **75.5** |
| ffn_down (Q4_1) | 59.0 | 67.1 | — | — |
| attn_qkv (Q4_0) | 61.6 | 69.1 | 70.5 | **76.0** |
| attn_gate (Q4_0) | 68.5 | 78.8 | 81.4 | **85.5** |
| ssm_out (Q5_K) | 53.3 | 69.4 | — | — |
| attn_q (Q4_0) | 68.6 | 77.9 | 80.3 | **84.3** |
| attn_output (Q4_0) | 57.7 | 67.8 | 69.5 | **73.8** |

## Round 2 (same day): driver constraints, thermal limits, BK=64

### Further measurements (separate runs, 8 s warm-up, all bitwise-equal)

Separate runs turned out to drift by ±3–4% with thermal state (see "Thermal state"
below). Only the interleaved races at the end of this section are comparisons.

1. **XDIRECT ablations** (1× = XDIRECT). The last column is the share of the WMMA peak
   at the measured clock (96 CUs × 512 FLOP/clk).

   | Work removed | ffn_gate | attn_qkv | attn_output | Clock | Peak share (ffn_gate) |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | Nothing (cfxh) | 84.7 | 78.0 | 76.5 | 2743 MHz | 63% |
   | A fragment loads (LDS) | 118.0 | 106.7 | 101.0 | 3030 MHz | 79% |
   | Barrier (incorrect results) | 91.7 | 84.7 | 83.7 | 2594 MHz | 72% |
   | Dequantization | 97.7 | 87.8 | 87.6 | 3001 MHz | 66% |
   | B fragment loads (global) | 89.3 | 79.7 | 79.9 | 2816 MHz | 65% |

   - A-side LDS fragment loads and the per-step barrier are the largest losses per clock.
   - Dequantization is mostly a power cost: removing it raises the clock by about
     260 MHz, but the per-clock share barely changes.
2. **Sustained WMMA peak** (`bench/coopmat/peak.comp`, wave64, 8 register-resident
   chains, 13 s): **131 TFLOP/s at about 2.94 GHz and about 280 W**, 91% of the
   theoretical rate at that clock.
   - Our GEMMs run at 2.6–2.85 GHz, so the clock explains only about 5–10% of the gap.
     The rest is issue efficiency: 63–66% of peak per clock.
3. **x48** (XDIRECT with 4×2 waves of 32×128, halving A loads per wave): 74.6–84.1,
   equal to or slightly below cfx. 256 VGPRs, 5 subgroups per SIMD.
4. **APAD=4** (LDS row stride 36 halves; conflict-free for 16 lanes × 8 bytes): equal to
   cfx within noise. Bank conflicts are not the A-path cost.
5. **`ACO_DEBUG=nosched`** (source order, no ACO scheduling) on cfx: 82.6 / 75.7 / 73.2,
   equal within noise. The instruction order inside a wave is not the lever.
6. **Do WMMA operands in lanes 16–31 matter?** A probe overwrote lanes 16–31 of B
   (`PROBE_B_HI`) or of A (`PROBE_A_HI`) with other values. Both gave
   `bitwise=False`, so **the hardware reads the replicated half-wave**. Operands cannot
   be loaded for 16 lanes only.
7. **In-loop descriptor reload.**
   - cfx's ISA reloads X's buffer descriptor (`s_load_b128 … 0x30`) in every k-step.
     The loop's first use of binding 3 is inside the loop, and NIR does not hoist it.
     It then waits with `lgkmcnt(0)`.
   - `XHOIST` (read `x16.length()` in the prologue to clamp row starts, a no-op for
     valid dispatches) moves the load out of the loop. ISA verified.
   - Speed effect: none within noise (race below).

You are a concise engineering assistant for the zerv project. The project's design documents follow; answer questions about them in at most three sentences.

4-wave workgroups (`g64`: 64×256 with 1×4 waves; `g128`: 128×128 with 2×2), so
     that two workgroups share a CU: 5–12% slower.
   - 32×64 wave tiles with 192 VGPRs and 8 subgroups per SIMD (`t24`: 64×256 with 2×4
     waves; `t42`: 128×128 with 4×2, the Mojo shape): no gain. In the race, t24 is
     1–4% below cfx.
9. **BK=64** (`k64`: two Q4_0 blocks per LDS stage, half the barriers per K; 36 KB
   LDS, 256 VGPRs): best variant, +0–4% over cfx in the race.
   - Process note: the first k64 build returned **bitwise=False** (50% of outputs NaN).
     `A_PER` was computed in an `#if` that used `HQ` before `HQ` was defined; an
     undefined macro evaluates to 0 in `#if`. So only half of the A rows were staged
     whenever `A_PER` = 2 (`dbg1`–`dbg3` confirmed it; the pre-edit source passed).
   - The bitwise gate caught it. After the fix, all shapes are bitwise-equal.

### Driver facts (Mesa 26.2.3 source, `third_party/mesa/mesa-26.2.3`)

Tarball from `archive.mesa3d.org`, sha256 `1628058a…` (full hash in
[hashes.sha256](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/hashes.sha256)); version as installed.

- **LDS loads are capped at 8 bytes.**
  - `src/amd/common/nir/ac_nir_lower_mem_access_bit_sizes.c`: "Don't use >64-bit LDS
    loads for performance reasons" (loads up to 8 bytes, stores up to 16).
  - `nir_opt_load_store_vectorize.c` `try_vectorize_shared2` pairs loads only at
    4 bytes (`ds_load_2addr_b32`).
  - So every 32-byte fragment costs four `ds_load_b64`, whatever the GLSL types.
- **Shaders that use LDS run in CU mode.** `radv_should_use_wgp_mode`: "LDS is faster
  with CU mode". Consequences:
  - An 8-wave workgroup occupies 4 waves on each of a CU's 2 SIMDs.
  - At 256 VGPRs the wave32 limit is 5 per SIMD: the allocation granule is 24 VGPRs,
    and 256 rounds up to 264.
  - So exactly one 128×256 workgroup runs per CU, and all 4 waves on a SIMD are in
    lockstep at every barrier. The occupancy variants above tested this; it did not
    turn into speed.
- **No `s_setprio` from SPIR-V.** rocm_wmma_gemm raises the wave priority around each
  WMMA. ACO only emits `s_setprio` for its own purposes.

### Thermal state

- The harness now also records the junction temperature and vddgfx.
- During sustained GEMMs the **junction sits at 110 °C** (the limit) at 310–339 W, with
  vddgfx at 966–1007 mV. The clock is therefore bounded by the thermal limit as well as
  the 339 W cap.
- Consecutive separate runs of the same module differ by up to about 4% (cfxh
  attn_gate: 87.6, then 89.6).
- New harness **[bench/race_gemm_f16.py](../../bench/race_gemm_f16.py)**:
  - one untimed 15 s heat soak;
  - then every variant on every tensor in each round, with the variant order rotated
    per round;
  - per-round ratios against the first variant, and the bitwise gate on round 0.

### Interleaved races (3 rounds, 3 s warm-up after the soak)

[Race r1](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab/races/r1/summary.json), ratios against cfx
(median [min..max]):

kernel (TFLOP/s median; ratio median [min..max]); all bitwise-equal:

| Shape (512 rows) | Shipped | cfx | **k64** |

- **k64** = `WAVE=32, WAVES_M=2, WAVES_N=4, BN=256, BK=64, FASTDQ, XDIRECT, XHOIST`,

- It is **1.25–1.36× the shipped kernel** on the Q4_0 shapes, bitwise-equal. It is the
  integration candidate.

  and k64 identical SPIR-V. The t24 module timed here came from an earlier revision;
  its SPIR-V hash is recorded.

### External references read this round (2026-09-24)

- **rocm_wmma_gemm** (github.com/adelj88/rocm_wmma_gemm @ `ea3aa74f`, HIP/LLVM, pinned
  under `third_party/research-gemm/`).
  - RX 7900 GRE f16: 83–86 TFLOP/s at 4096×5120×5120-class shapes, 74–77 at 4096³ and
    8192³ (their `docs/gfx1100_*.md`).
  - Techniques:
    - LDS fragment loads issued one WMMA ahead, in a snake order;
    - global prefetch split into chunks between WMMAs;
    - `s_setprio(1)` around each WMMA;
    - `k_slices` 2–4 (BK = 32–64);
    - `single_buffer` (one LDS stage) where occupancy wins;
    - tuned 4×2 or 2×4 wave layouts of 4×4 WMMA tiles.
  - The first two need scheduling control that ACO does not give us; see the driver
    facts for `s_setprio`.
- **hipfire** (github.com/warpfront/hipfire @ `ad10b3d9`, Rust+HIP, a 7900 XTX engine
  that serves Qwen 3.x) is a potential competitor.
  - Its own historical table: Qwen 3.5 27B MQ4 prefill peak **478 tok/s**, decode
    47 tok/s. For comparison, our f16 mode prefills 3223 tokens at about 910 tok/s and
    decodes at 54 tok/s.
  - It uses its own quantization format, so it is not an equivalent-weights comparison.
    Its DFlash speculative decoding is relevant to block 17.

## Consequences and next steps

- **XDIRECT requires f16 X in memory.** In the model, the kernels producing GEMM inputs
  (norms, SwiGLU, gates) would write an f16 copy with the same RNE rounding the GEMM
  applies today. That is bitwise-neutral, and it fits the fusion work (16c).
- **Integration candidate: k64** (round 2). Q4_1 and Q5_K need the same structure.
  FASTDQ is only bit-identical for Q4_0, because the Q4_1/Q5_K formulas round twice in
  the shipped kernel, so those formats keep their shipped dequantization.
- **Where the rest of the gap is:**
  - Per clock, the kernel reaches about 63% of the WMMA peak. The A-side LDS fragment
    loads and the per-step barrier are the measured losses.
  - Under this driver, the known remedies need scheduling control (fine interleave,
    `s_setprio`) or wider LDS loads, and neither is available (driver facts above).
  - The card also runs at its thermal limit. So further gains must come from less
    energy per FLOP (less data movement) as well as from fewer stalls.
- **Remaining levers, not yet tried:**
  - Aligned (repacked) weight loads. Today each half-block needs 5 dword loads and
    selects.
  - Larger BN, so weights are dequantized once per GEMM.
  - Rows 32–256 (smaller plans) and a device-keyed tile table.
  - An own ISA backend is the route to the scheduling control; it would be a decision
    under D5 and is not approved.
- **Not claimed yet:** no model-level or serving number. These are component timings
  only.

# Hand-scheduled RDNA3 machine code for `gemm_f16x` (2026-09-24)

Question: how much faster can the f16 prefill GEMM (`src/model/gemm_f16x.comp`, Q4_0 × f16 X →
f32, WMMA 16×16×16, wave32, tile 128×256, BK 64) get when we write its machine code ourselves and
load it through `VK_KHR_pipeline_binary` (decision D7 in [design/speed.md](../design/speed.md);
mechanism in [native-isa-via-vulkan.md](../research/native-isa-via-vulkan.md))? Adoption bar:
≥ 1.2× the SPIR-V kernel, bit-identical outputs.

**Answer: 1.20–1.23× at 512 rows and 1.22–1.40× at the 3,328-row plan of the 3,223-token
prompt (component), bit-identical on every output tested. Integrated as `--gemm-code native`
(default; `spirv` keeps the previous kernel): f16-mode TTFT −12% at 836 and 3,223 tokens and
−10% at 12k tokens, served outputs byte-identical** (section "Integration").

## Setup

- Device: RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), Mesa 26.2.3 RADV (`mesa 1:26.2.3-1`), power cap 339 W, `auto`
  performance level. clang 22.1.8 (`-target amdgcn-mesa-mesa3d -mcpu=gfx1100`) as the assembler.
- Kernel source: [bench/isa_lab/gen_f16x.py](../../bench/isa_lab/gen_f16x.py) generates the whole
  kernel (prologue, loop, epilogue) as assembler source; the shipped result is
  [data/…/gemm_f16x_q4_0-v4.s](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x-isa/gemm_f16x_q4_0-v4.s).
  `isa_tool.py asm` assembles it; `isa_tool.py splice` puts the code into the RADV pipeline binary
  of the SPIR-V kernel (`pipeline_binary_lab dump`), config unchanged: 256 VGPRs, 108 SGPRs,
  36,864 B LDS, CU mode (RADV uses `config.rsrc1/2/3` verbatim: `radv_shader_create_uncached`).
- Lab: [bench/isa_lab/pipeline_binary_lab.c](../../bench/isa_lab/pipeline_binary_lab.c) (reference =
  SPIR-V pipeline or another binary; random Q4_0 weights and f16 X in VRAM; parameters m, k, rows,
  n, seed, abase, xbase, sub, batch, dump, iodev), [race.py](../../bench/isa_lab/race.py) (warm-up,
  sysfs sampler during the timed reps), [sweep.py](../../bench/isa_lab/sweep.py) (bitwise matrix).
- Hashes of every input and tool: [hashes.sha256](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x-isa/hashes.sha256).

## Correctness gate

The arithmetic is the SPIR-V kernel's, by construction: each accumulator gets its WMMAs in
ascending k (part 0..3 of each stage, stages ascending); each weight is `pk_mul(pk_add(0x6400|q,
−1032), d)` with the same f16 ops; only the integer extraction (`v_perm_b32` + `v_and_or_b32`
instead of shifts/selects) and data movement differ.

`sweep.py` ([bitwise-v4.jsonl](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x-isa/bitwise-v4.jsonl)): **23
configurations, 91 M outputs, 0 different** — all six model Q4_0 shapes at 512 rows and at 768 plan
rows with n = 700 (row tail), misaligned blocks (abase = 2), an X offset (xbase = 8) and 2%
f16-subnormal scales; K = 64 (one stage), 128, 192, 320 (odd stage counts), n = 1, 17, 255, 257,
300; 50% subnormal scales; M = 128. The whole plan is compared, including rows ≥ n (they read row
n − 1). Every intermediate variant below that is not labelled an ablation passed the same kind of
check before it was timed.

## Results

Interleaved races (`race.py`, 8 s warm-up, 31 reps × 5 dispatches per side, 3 rounds with
different seeds), [raw](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x-isa/race-v4.jsonl). TFLOP/s median:

| Tensor | M×K | Rows | SPIR-V | **v4** | Ratio median [min..max] |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ffn_gate/up | 17408×5120 | 512 | 71.5 | 87.3 | **1.216** [1.214..1.229] |
| ffn_gate/up | 17408×5120 | 3328 | 83.5 | 101.9 | **1.220** [1.214..1.228] |
| ffn_down | 5120×17408 | 512 | 67.0 | 79.6 | **1.204** [1.183..1.224] |
| ffn_down | 5120×17408 | 3328 | 76.5 | 97.3 | **1.273** [1.270..1.274] |
| attn_qkv | 10240×5120 | 512 | 64.0 | 77.4 | **1.212** [1.206..1.212] |
| attn_qkv | 10240×5120 | 3328 | 79.0 | 99.0 | **1.253** [1.218..1.253] |
| attn_gate | 6144×5120 | 512 | 71.6 | 86.5 | **1.207** [1.207..1.210] |
| attn_gate | 6144×5120 | 3328 | 64.7 | 90.6 | **1.401** [1.399..1.406] |
| attn_q | 12288×5120 | 512 | 73.4 | 88.1 | **1.204** [1.201..1.218] |
| attn_q | 12288×5120 | 3328 | 70.3 | 98.4 | **1.398** [1.395..1.400] |
| attn_output | 5120×6144 | 512 | 63.6 | 76.5 | **1.209** [1.203..1.209] |
| attn_output | 5120×6144 | 3328 | 65.7 | 89.3 | **1.352** [1.342..1.362] |

Board power and clock are in the raw lines (512 rows: ~170–220 W, 2.1–2.3 GHz; 3,328 rows:
240–320 W, 2.4–2.5 GHz). Components only; the ratio in the model is still to be measured.

## What the kernel does (v4)

- **Addressing without VALU.** The loop is unrolled by two stages, so every LDS offset (stage,
  fragment, part) is an immediate. X and A-block addresses are per-lane constants plus an SGPR
  `soffset` (X: +256 B per two stages; A: +72 B). Q4_0 block alignment (`addr & 2`) is constant
  over K (36 B per stage), so it becomes two per-lane `v_perm_b32` selectors and a scale shift.
- **One Q4_0 block per thread per stage** (row tid/2, block tid%2): 1 × (b128 + b32) raw load,
  65 VALU ops for 32 weights (ACO: ~130), 4 × `ds_store_b128`.
- **A fragments: 2 × `ds_load_b128`** per fragment (ACO: 4 × `ds_load_b64`; its NIR caps LDS
  loads at 8 bytes). Row stride 144 B is conflict-free for 16 lanes × 16 B.
- **Software pipeline, i-major WMMA order.** A single-buffered (A_i of part q+1 is loaded right
  after its last use in part q: 12 WMMAs of slack); B double-buffered in registers (B_j of part
  q+2 loaded after its last use in part q: 20 WMMAs of slack). The next stage's raw A is fetched
  at the start of the stage and dequantized/stored during part 2; the single barrier sits in
  part 3 after the first four WMMAs, just before the next stage's first A loads (all RAW/WAR
  constraints between the two LDS buffers hold across waves). No register shuffles.
- **Every `s_waitcnt` is computed** by a simulator in the generator (both counters complete in
  order; no SMEM in the loop), which also checks that each stage exits in exactly its entry
  state. It rejected one variant (WMMA order `diag`) whose B loads leave in a different order.
- **Barrier as ACO does in CU mode:** `s_waitcnt_depctr vm_vsrc(0)` + `s_barrier` (LDS executes a
  workgroup's requests in order; `aco_insert_waitcnt.cpp` `finish_barrier_internal`).
- **Epilogue through LDS** (see finding 3): each wave stages 32 m × 16 tokens in its 2,304 B slice
  of the LDS buffer the last stage did not read (no extra barrier needed) and writes 32
  `buffer_store_b128` per wave (4 full 128 B lines each) instead of 128 `buffer_store_b32`.
- **Row count read late** (finding 4); `s_setprio 1` around each WMMA (+0.3 to +1.3%, 4 of 4
  races positive).

## Findings, in order (including negative results)

1. **v1 (pipeline, b128 LDS loads, cheap dequant, ACO-style epilogue): bit-identical, only
   1.07× (ffn_gate 17408×5120), 1.13× (ffn_down), 1.07× (attn_q).** Ablations (results wrong,
   timing only, sustained, vs v1): no dequant VALU 1.03, no barrier 1.01, no A loads 1.00, no B
   loads 0.99, everything except the WMMAs removed 1.17. Added back one at a time onto the
   WMMA-only loop: dequant −2%, A loads −4%, B loads −7%, raw loads −6%, **barrier alone −12%**.
2. **The barrier "cost" did not scale with the number of barriers**: one per two stages, one per
   stage and two per stage all cost 11–12%, independent of the `depctr` wait, the LDS stores, the
   position in the stage, WMMA operand order and `s_setprio`. Per-wave probes (HW_ID and
   `MSG_RTN_GET_REALTIME` stamps, `--probe`, `abl=stamp`) showed:
   - waves of a workgroup alternate between two SIMDs (4 + 4), two workgroups per WGP;
   - **without barriers the SIMD arbiter is strictly age-ordered**: waves 0/1 finish their whole
     K loop first (≈ 1/4 of the workgroup time), then 2/3, 4/5, 6/7; one wave saturates the
     WMMA pipe on its own (1, 2, 3, 4 active waves per SIMD: 109, 217, 339, 444 µs);
   - so free-running waves finish staggered, while any barrier makes all 8 finish together.
3. **The real cost was the epilogue store burst.** With the result stores removed, v1 is
   **1.15× faster**, and the barrier variant equals the free-running one. The SPIR-V store pattern
   (`coopMatStore`, also ours in v1) issues 128 `buffer_store_b32` per lane, each touching 16
   cache lines with 8 bytes, and all 96 workgroups of a round issue them at the same moment.
   Free-running waves had hidden it by storing while others computed. **v2 (epilogue through
   LDS): 1.117× v1**; the epilogue now costs 1.6%.
4. **Dispatch start: the row count in host memory.** Stamps inside the prologue: the first scalar
   loads take **15.4 µs in the first round of every dispatch and 0.4 µs afterwards**, and 0.52 µs
   when the lab puts `io` in device memory (`iodev=1`). All 768 waves of the first round read
   `n` from the host-visible `io` buffer at once (zerv also keeps `io` in `.host` memory). v3 issues
   the load first, does the stage-0 fetch/dequant/barrier meanwhile, loads the first B fragments
   with unclamped rows and reloads them clamped only if the tile reaches past n: the dispatch
   span drops by ~10 µs (1050 → 1040 µs, probe), ~1%, below the race noise. **This affects every
   zerv kernel that reads `io` at dispatch start**; not acted on here (see "Open").
5. Other variants, bit-identical, vs v3 (one sustained race each unless noted): `s_setprio` around
   WMMAs **+0.3 to +1.3% (4 races) → adopted (v4)**; dequant in part 1 −1.4%; j-major WMMA order
   −0.6%. Earlier (v1): cold-A tile prefetch was not needed — the slow start was finding 4.
6. **Remaining gap (v2/v3):** the WMMA-only loop with the new epilogue is 1.064× v2; of that the
   dequant VALU is ~4% (65 VALU per 64 WMMAs per wave: ACO models a gfx11 f16 WMMA as 32 VALU
   cycles, so each VALU op is pure additional SIMD time), the epilogue 1.6%. Loads and barrier are
   within noise. The WMMA-only loop itself runs at ~89% of 512 FLOP/clk/CU, close to the 91%
   peak probe. At 512 rows, 272 tiles on 96 CUs also lose ~5.6% to the last partial round; that
   cannot be balanced without changing the per-output accumulation order.

## Measurement notes

- **Single-dispatch timing misleads.** The first lab races (one dispatch per side per rep) gave
  different ratios and ~15% lower absolute numbers than batched (sustained) timing; all numbers
  above use `batch ≥ 5`. The clock ramps between fences otherwise.
- The sampler reads `freq1_input`/`power1_average` only during the timed reps; the averages are
  coarse (tens of samples).
- Ablation and probe numbers in findings 1–6 come from single interleaved races (21–61 reps,
  batch 10); their raw lines were not kept, only the numbers quoted here. The adoption table
  above is the controlled measurement.

## Commands

```sh
cc -std=gnu11 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Ithird_party/vulkan/1.4.354/include \
  bench/isa_lab/pipeline_binary_lab.c -lvulkan -lm -o third_party/isa-lab/pipeline_binary_lab
cd third_party/isa-lab && ./pipeline_binary_lab dump ../../src/model/shaders/gemm_f16x_q4_0.spv f16x-aco
python3 ../../bench/isa_lab/gen_f16x.py gen/v4.s
python3 ../../bench/isa_lab/isa_tool.py asm gen/v4.s gen/v4.code
python3 ../../bench/isa_lab/isa_tool.py splice f16x-aco.bin gen/v4.code gen/v4.bin && cp f16x-aco.key gen/v4.key
cd ../..
python3 bench/isa_lab/sweep.py src/model/shaders/gemm_f16x_q4_0.spv third_party/isa-lab/gen/v4.bin OUT.jsonl
python3 bench/isa_lab/race.py src/model/shaders/gemm_f16x_q4_0.spv third_party/isa-lab/gen/v4.bin \
  reps=31 batch=5 rows=3328 seed=1 m=17408 k=5120 --warm 8
```

Ablations: `gen_f16x.py OUT.s --abl nodq,nobar,noa,nob,noraw,noepi,…`; probes: `--probe`
(+ `--abl …,stamp`), lab `dump=FILE`.

## Integration (same day)

Spec: [prefill.md, "Native gemm_f16x machine code"](../specs/prefill.md) and
[gpu-driver.md, "Pipeline binaries"](../specs/gpu-driver.md), written before the code.

- **Driver** (`src/gpu`): `Device.Options.pipeline_binaries` enables `VK_KHR_pipeline_binary`

  constants, all 56/79 old records unchanged.
- **Artifacts** `src/model/native/` built by `tools/build_native_gemm.py` (fresh dump → gen →

- **Knob** `--gemm-code native|spirv` (server default `native`; `Model.Options.gemm_code`), also

# f16 prefill: wave32 GEMM on f16 X integrated for Q4_0 (block 16b, 2026-09-24)

Question: does the lab kernel k64 ([lab report](2026-09-24-gemm-f16-lab.md)) speed up
f16-mode prefill end to end without changing a single output bit? And where does zerv
now stand against llama-server's default fast path?

Spec: [prefill.md, "f16 GEMM, wave32 kernel with f16 X"](../specs/prefill.md).

## What changed

- **`src/model/gemm_f16x.comp`**: the k64 structure.
  - wave32 with required subgroup size and full subgroups;
  - 2×4 waves of 64×64, tile 128×256, BK 64;
  - Q4_0 dequantized once per workgroup into LDS with the exact `0x6400|q` bit trick;
  - B fragments loaded straight from an f16 copy of X;
  - X's descriptor used before the loop, so it is not reloaded per k-step.
- **Selection** `gemm.f16Kernel`:
  - Q4_0 with M ≥ 4096, K % 64 == 0 and plan rows % 256 == 0 → `gemm_f16x`;
  - other f16 projections (Q4_1, Q5_K, the 128-row plan) → `gemm_f16` (block 14);
  - small shapes stay FP32.
- **Validation** `gemm.validateF16x`. The weight checks are factored out of `validate`
  (`checkA`) and shared.
- **f16 X copies:**
  - `model.comp` built with `F16OUT` gives the `norm_h`, `swiglu_h` and `gate_h`
    producers. They store `float16_t(y)` of the FP32 value they write into the arena
    region `x16` (rows × ffn halves, reused by one input at a time).
  - The runtime uses them only when a consumer in the next GEMM phase runs `gemm_f16x`.
  - The FP32 modules are **byte-identical** to before (`compile_model.py`; the four new
    modules are the only additions).
- **GPU layer:**
  - `Kernel.Options.full_subgroups` (`REQUIRE_FULL_SUBGROUPS`). The device enables
    `computeFullSubgroups` with subgroup size control.
  - The binding constant was regenerated twice, identically, from the pinned registry;
    the ABI fixture now has 56 structs and 78 constants.
  - The kernel cap rose from 64 to 128 (`gpu.max_kernels`): f16 mode now needs 71
    kernels on 4 weight banks, and FP32 needs 55.
  - `gemm.deviceNeeds(precision)` gives the device features for the server and tools.

## Verification (all executed)

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1. `gemm_f16x` vs `gemm_f16` on random Q4_0 (scales with f16-subnormal products and subnormal d; negative and large scales), K = 64 / 512 / 5120, n = 256 / 200 / 1 / 256 | **bitwise equal** on all valid rows; FP64 bound holds on samples; no writes past the plan |
| Selection and validation (rows 128 → `gemm_f16`, Q4_1, K % 64, x alignment, x_rs < K, split-K, a_rs, A / Y extents) | pass |
| Full-subgroup kernel on a device without subgroup size control | `UnsupportedFeature` |
| 2. `norm_h` (with residual add, row tail), `swiglu_h` (odd half offset), `gate_h`: f16 copy = f16(FP32 output) | **bitwise**, all elements; FP32 outputs match an FP64 reference; sentinels untouched |
| 3. `verify_model.py --precision f16 --modes 512,128`, default and long oracles | `logits.bin`, `serving-logits.bin` and `tensors.bin` hashes **identical** to the block-14 reports in every case and mode; only timings differ |
| 4. Serving outputs, old vs new f16 build | **byte-identical** (`output_sha256`), all 12 serving-v2 requests and 3 requests at 12k |
| `zig build test` (Debug, ReleaseFast) 81/81; `gpu-test` (Debug, ReleaseFast) 22/22; Python unittest 53; `zig fmt --check` | pass |

- Gate 1 found one contract detail. For rows ≥ n (plan rows nobody reads), `gemm_f16`
  skips 128-row tiles at or past n, while `gemm_f16x` computes them from row n − 1.
  Both stay inside the plan, so the bitwise gate is on rows < n.
- Gate-3 data:
  - [default](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/verify-f16-default-mode512.json),
    [default mode 128](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/verify-f16-default-mode128.json);
  - [long](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/verify-f16-long-mode512.json),
    [long mode 128](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/verify-f16-long-mode128.json);
  - compared against [block 14's reports](data/2026-09-24-f16-prefill/).
- Process failure, retained: the first gate-3 run failed at model load with
  `ResourceLimit`, because f16 mode needs 71 kernels and the cap was 64. Fixed by the
  raised cap above; spec updated in [gpu-driver.md](../specs/gpu-driver.md).

## Performance

Setup:

- RX 7900 XTX, Mesa 26.2.3; model sha `ede16c7b…`.
- Binaries: new zerv `72b986c3…`; old zerv `fd3f6770…` (the serving-fixes build, the
  last before 16b); llama-server build 10964 (`b29c606e`), binary `0f401589…`.
- Engines ran one at a time on an otherwise idle host. Full hashes are in
  [hashes.sha256](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/hashes.sha256), with manifests next to
  each run.
- The card runs these loads at the 110 °C junction limit
  ([hardware](../hardware.md)).

### Per-phase GPU time, 3223 tokens

`zerv-model-profile MODEL 4096 512 3223 16 f16`, one run
([new](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/profile-f16-p3223.jsonl),
[block 14](data/2026-09-24-f16-prefill/profile-f16-p3223.jsonl)).

| Phase (sum over the prefill) | Block 14 | Now | Ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ffn_in (gate + up, Q4_0) | 1169.7 ms | 866.7 ms | 0.741 |
| ffn_down (Q4_0 and Q4_1 layers) | 719.6 | 561.2 | 0.780 |
| lin_in (qkv, z, α, β) | 479.5 | 374.8 | 0.782 |
| attn_in (q, k, v) | 137.6 | 111.8 | 0.813 |
| attn_out | 63.9 | 47.8 | 0.749 |
| lin_out (ssm_out, Q5_K, not ported) | 202.0 | 201.3 | 0.996 |
| norm (+ f16 copy) | 26.7 | 29.9 | 1.118 |
| swiglu (+ f16 copy) | 39.4 | 45.3 | 1.150 |
| **Total prefill GPU time** | **3509.3** | **2888.9** | **0.823** |

The per-chunk time for 512-row chunks went from 519–578 ms to 416–476 ms.

### Serving (serving-v2, 3 repeats)

`cd bench && python3 run_serving.py --output ../docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/serving-run1
--zerv-binary ../third_party/gemm-f16x/zerv-72b986c3 --engines zerv-f16,llama-fa-ub512`,
then the same with `--output …/serving-old-run1 --zerv-binary
../third_party/serving-fixes/zerv-fd3f6770 --engines zerv-f16`.

| Case (prompt tokens) | zerv f16 before (ms) | **zerv f16 now** (ms) | llama-server default (ms) | Now / before | llama / now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| short-nothink (23) | 143 / 143 / 143 | 143 / 144 / 143 | 162 / 161 / 161 | 1.00 | 1.13 |
| decode-think (81) | 307 / 307 / 308 | 305 / 307 / 307 | 372 / 370 / 366 | 1.00 | 1.21 |
| medium-prompt (836) | 1054 / 1064 / 1071 | **940 / 946 / 952** | 1193 / 1196 / 1207 | **0.89** | **1.26** |
| long-prompt (3223) | 3610 / 3624 / 3641 | **3023 / 3036 / 3050** | 3376 / 3392 / 3398 | **0.84** | **1.12** |

Decode (tok/s) did not change: zerv 54 / 49 / 49 / 56, llama 44 / 41 / 41 / 45.

### Serving at 12,034 prompt tokens

`python3 run_long_context.py --paragraphs 60 --engines zerv-f16,llama-fa-ub512 …`, one
warm-up plus two timed requests per engine, context 29,504.
Data: [new + llama](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/serving-p12k/),
[old](data/2026-09-24-gemm-f16x/serving-p12k-old/).

| Engine | TTFT (s), 3 requests | Decode tok/s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| zerv f16 before | 15.07 / 15.08 / 15.14 | 44.7 / 44.4 / 44.5 |
| **zerv f16 now** | **12.91 / 12.92 / 12.98** | 44.7 / 44.6 / 44.6 |
| llama-server default | 12.44 / 12.46 / 12.49 | 39.3 / 39.2 / 39.3 |

## Interpretation

- **The GEMM gain carries through end to end, bit-exactly:** −18% prefill GPU time and
  −16% TTFT at 3223 tokens, −14% at 12k.
- **Against llama-server's default fast path** (f16 WMMA with f16 accumulation, less
  precise than zerv's f32 accumulation):
  - zerv f16 is **1.12× faster at 3223 tokens** (it was 1.04× slower) and 1.26× faster
    at 836;
  - **3.6% slower at 12k**. The remaining long-prompt loss is prefill attention: the
    materialized-score FP32 path grows with position (`scores` + `pv` = 264 ms of the
    2.9 s at 3223 tokens). That is block 16a.
- **Precision caveat:** zerv f16 still fails block 14's quality gate 2 on the single
  worst token of long-think; see [f16 prefill](2026-09-24-f16-prefill.md) and design
  question Q1. This change did not alter a bit of it.
- **Next GEMM steps:**
  - Q4_1 (part of ffn_down) and Q5_K (ssm_out, 201 ms, unchanged) on the same
    structure;
  - the 128-row plan;
  - the M = 5120 shapes, which fill 83% of the last round of workgroups on 96 CUs.

# Host-resident embedding and prefix-cache snapshots (2026-09-24)

Question: VRAM bounds the context (FP32 KV, 128 KiB per token). Which large buffers can
live in system memory, what does that cost in TTFT and decode, and what should the
defaults be? Knobs: `--embedding-memory host|device` and `--prefix-cache-memory
device|host` ([model spec](../specs/model.md), "Host-resident data";
[prefix cache spec](../specs/prefix-cache.md)).

## Setup

- RX 7900 XTX, Mesa 26.2.3 RADV, PCIe 4.0 x16; Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0 (sha256 `ede16c7b…`).
- zerv binary sha256 `cfbc6e0738292cda…` (both serving runs; the manifests hold the full
  hashes and commands).
- The token embedding (Q4_0, 682 MiB) is read one 2,880-byte row per token by `embed`
  and `embed_b`. A snapshot slot is 156,893,184 bytes (all DeltaNet and conv state); the
  server keeps 8 slots by default (1,197 MiB).

## Correctness (all run with the new code; raw files in [data](data/2026-09-24-host-memory/))

| Gate | Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tools/verify_model.py`, default oracle, modes 0/1/13/512/512:17 | host embedding | passes; all 28 capture and logit files byte-identical to the previous device-embedding captures (`third_party/model-native/2026-09-24-flash-final-default`) |
| `zerv-prefix-check` fp32 | host snapshots | gate passed: restore = split bitwise at 11 points, repeat and extend bitwise |
| `zerv-prefix-check` fp32 | device snapshots | gate passed |
| `zerv-prefix-check` f16 | host snapshots | gate passed |
| `zerv-spec-check` | host embedding | 11/11 cases: verify rows, committed state and follow-up decode bitwise equal to decode |
| `zerv-mtp-check` + FP64 reference | host embedding | both sequences pass (bound 1e-5) |
| serving-v2, 8 engine runs | all combinations | every case has one output hash across all engines |

The prefix check was changed in this step. It now compares restore with split directly
(`restore_vs_split`) and exits non-zero unless that gate holds. Earlier it only compared
both with the cold run, which differs off the chunk grid. It also takes
`[host|device]` and times the copies.

Process note: the first two prefix-check runs of this step used a stale
`zig-out/bin/zerv-prefix-check` built before the change: the default `zig build` step
runs tests and does not install tools. They are discarded. The tools were rebuilt with
their `*-build` steps (`prefix-check-build`, `spec-check-build`, `mtp-check-build`) before
the runs above.

## Snapshot copy cost (`zerv-prefix-check MODEL fp32 host|device`, 20 timed copies)

| Slot memory | save ms (median, min–max) | load ms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| device | 0.476 (0.464–0.530) | 0.452 (0.440–0.476) |
| host | 9.805 (9.771–9.841) | 15.285 (15.260–15.325) |

Host copies run at 16.0 GB/s (save, VRAM → RAM) and 10.3 GB/s (load).

  (one or two 9.8 ms saves on the prefill path), no decode cost**, 1,197 MiB less VRAM
  at 8 slots. That is 7% of short-request TTFT. **Default: device** (fastest); `--prefix-cache-memory

  prefill path), then copy to the host on a transfer queue while compute continues.

# Host overhead of decode and speculative decode (2026-09-24)

Question (user guidance: look for CPU-side optimizations, comptime where it pays off, but
measure first): how much of decode time is host work, and is any of it worth specializing?

## Instrumentation

`session.Result` now carries `backend_ns` (time inside backend `step`/`draft`/`verify`/
`commit` calls: submission, GPU work and fence wait) and `sample_ns` (time inside the
sampler) next to `decode_ns`. The server logs one line per request:
`decode time: T ms total, B ms in backend calls, S ms sampling, O ms other host work`
(O = token handling: detokenizing, UTF-8, stop strings, reasoning split, streaming).
Cost: three to six clock reads per token.

## Measurement

`python3 bench/run_serving.py --workload bench/workloads/decode-v1.json --output
docs/bench/data/2026-09-24-host-overhead/decode-v1 --engines "zerv,zerv-spec3" --repeats 1`
(greedy, 512 tokens; server logs in the data directory):

| engine | case | total ms | backend | sampling | other host |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3 drafts | code | 4,180 | 4,144 (99.14%) | 30.0 (0.72%) | 5.8 (0.14%) |
| 3 drafts | json | 4,044 | 4,006 (99.06%) | 31.6 (0.78%) | 6.4 (0.16%) |
| 3 drafts | think | 4,715 | 4,677 (99.19%) | 31.6 (0.67%) | 6.5 (0.14%) |
| 3 drafts | prose | 6,688 | 6,650 (99.43%) | 31.6 (0.47%) | 6.8 (0.10%) |
| plain | 4 cases | 10,065–10,109 | 99.5–99.6% | 31.6–35.6 (0.31–0.35%) | 7.7–13.7 (0.08–0.14%) |

- Sampling is about 60 µs per token: the greedy scan of one 248,320-float logits row
  (1 MB of mapped host memory) at about 17 GB/s, close to one core's memory bandwidth.
  The component benchmark measured 49 µs for the same scan
  ([sampler](2026-09-24-sampler.md)).
- Cross-check with a cost model (per cycle: `draft(t, 3)` 4.67 ms from `zerv-mtp-check`,
  plus verify+commit at the average verified rows from `zerv-spec-check`; the earlier
  verify-fusion serving data): measured decode spans exceed the model by 0.54–0.93 ms per
  cycle (1.8–3.1%). The breakdown above puts 99% of the time inside backend calls, so
  most of that gap is GPU time and submission latency at serving positions and commit
  sizes, not session host work.
- Inside the backend calls, each synchronous submit + fence wait costs about 50 µs of
  GPU idle ([driver bench](2026-09-22-gpu-driver.md): tiny-dispatch round trip). A
  speculative cycle has three (commit, draft, verify): about 0.15 ms of about 29 ms.

## Conclusion

Host-caused GPU idle is about 1.4% of a speculative cycle (sampling about 0.2 ms, three
round trips about 0.15 ms, token handling about 0.05 ms) and about 0.6% of a plain step.
No comptime or CPU specialization is warranted now: the sampler dispatch is a few
branches per token, and the scan is bandwidth-bound.

Candidates if this share ever matters (each under 1%, recorded in TODO.md):
- greedy without penalties: argmax of the verify rows on the GPU, reading 4–5 ids
  instead of 4–5 MB of logits (about 0.2 ms per cycle);
- commit and the next draft in one submission (both are known once the host has
  sampled): one round trip fewer per cycle (about 0.05 ms);
- a single-pass vectorized greedy argmax (one read of the row instead of max, then find;
  about 20 µs per token).

# Single-user decode on HyperQwen's protocol (2026-09-24)

Question (user): a Medium article claims 177 tok/s for Qwen3.8-27B on one RTX 3090. Are we that
much slower? Answer: the 177 is aggregate throughput of 8 concurrent requests. For **one user**,
HyperQwen's own README reports 120 / 111 tok/s (MTP, greedy / default sampling) on a 3090; on the
same protocol zerv reaches **91.3 / 79.5 tok/s** on the RX 7900 XTX, 34% above a tuned llama-server
with MTP on this machine. The gap to HyperQwen is the cost of a speculative step, not the base
decode (ours is faster).

## Setup

- Protocol: HyperQwen's single-user benchmark (README of github.com/syv-ai/HyperQwen @
  `1cf86656`; the numbers there are vLLM 0.27.1 measurements on an RTX 3090 at 250 W with its own
  ~20 GB requantization): the 8 prompts of `bench/prompts_real.jsonl` (sha256 `27da4fd8…`),
  1,024-token answers, one stream, the model's chat template with thinking on, model-default
  sampling (T 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20) and greedy. Decode = 1000 / mean TPOT.
- Workloads (ours, converted): [bench/workloads/hyperqwen-real-v1-greedy.json](../../bench/workloads/hyperqwen-real-v1-greedy.json),
  [-default.json](../../bench/workloads/hyperqwen-real-v1-default.json), `run_serving.py
  --engines zerv-f16-spec3,zerv-f16,llama-fa-ub512-mtp3 --repeats 1`, one engine at a time.
- zerv `c88642a1…` (f16 prefill, native GEMM; 3 drafts adaptive, or plain); llama-server build
  10964 (`b29c606e`) with `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 -fa on -b 2048 -ub 512`.
  Model sha `ede16c7b…`. Data: [greedy](data/2026-09-24-hyperqwen-protocol/greedy/),
  [default](data/2026-09-24-hyperqwen-protocol/default/) (manifests with all hashes and commands).

## Results

Decode tok/s (1000 / mean TPOT), 8 prompts:

| Engine | Greedy | Default sampling | Tokens per step (greedy / default) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **zerv, 3 MTP drafts** | **91.3** | **79.5** | 2.62 / 2.21 |
| zerv, plain | 50.9 | 51.2 | 1 |
| llama-server, MTP 3 | 68.2 | 59.8 | — |
| HyperQwen MTP (3090, their README) | 120.0 | 111.1 | 2.90 / 2.75 |
| HyperQwen DFlash2 (3090, their README) | 131.2 | 121.8 | 3.34 / 3.12 |
| HyperQwen plain (their batch mode, C1) | 45–46 | 45–46 | 1 |

Mean TTFT: zerv 222 ms, llama-server 405–563 ms (their README: 164 ms on the 3090 setup).
zerv's outputs: 7 of 8 answers use all 1,024 tokens.

## Interpretation

Not an equal-conditions comparison: different GPU, different quantization (their ~20 GB
requantization vs our 15.3 GB Q4_0), their numbers are from their README and not re-run here. But
the per-step arithmetic is informative:

- Plain step: zerv 19.6 ms, HyperQwen 21.7 ms (1/46).
- Speculative cycle (drafting + verification): zerv 91.3 / 2.62 → **28.7 ms, +46% over a plain
  step**; HyperQwen 120 / 2.90 → 24.2 ms, +12%.
- Our cycle, from earlier component measurements: verifying 3 rows costs 22.7 ms, and each draft
  ~1.55 ms, 80% of it the Q6_K output head ([draft-vocab report](2026-09-24-draft-vocab.md)).
  HyperQwen's README credits a calibrated draft vocabulary and requantized heads for its cheap
  draft.
- Acceptance under T = 1 sampling: we accept a draft only when the sampled token equals it, so
  speculative output is byte-identical to non-speculative output (our gate 3). vLLM uses
  rejection sampling: the same output distribution, higher acceptance (2.75 vs 2.21 tokens per
  step here), not seed-identical.

## Consequences (TODO.md)

1. **Draft cost** is the largest single-user decode lever: the frequency-ranked draft vocabulary
   (queued in 17c) with a representative, non-benchmark frequency source. Est. +10–15%.
2. **Distribution-exact speculative sampling** as an opt-in knob (rejection sampling). Est. +20%
   at T = 1; changes which sample is drawn, not the distribution; needs its own research and a
   statistical gate.
3. Multi-user: their 177 / ~400 / ~1,035 tok/s aggregate numbers need batched decode, which zerv
   does not have (the next block).

# KV buffers: context beyond the single 4 GiB state buffer (2026-09-24)

Question: can the KV cache leave the single ≤ 4 GiB state buffer without changing a bit, and
how much context does the card then hold?

Spec: [model.md, "KV buffers"](../specs/model.md). User request: "okay fix it".

## Why there was a cap

- Vulkan exposes at most `maxStorageBufferRange` = 4 GiB − 1 per storage-buffer binding
  (a 32-bit field). RADV on this card also caps one allocation and one buffer at 0xfffffffc
  (`vulkaninfo`: `maxMemoryAllocationSize`, `maxBufferSize`).
- zerv kept every attention layer's KV plus the recurrent state in one buffer (with a
  3.75 GiB margin), so context stopped at 29,523 tokens (27,786 with the MTP layer),
  whatever VRAM was free.

## Change

- The KV caches (16 trunk layers, then the MTP layer's) live in their own KV buffers, as
  many consecutive caches per buffer as fit 3.75 GiB (`layout.State`).
- The four kernels that touch the cache (`qkprep`, `qk_b`, `attn_scores`, `attn_pv`) and
  the prefill attention GEMM exist once per KV buffer, bound where the state arena was.
  **No shader changed**; the model modules are byte-identical.
- A command may now retain 64 distinct kernels (was 32).
- `Options.kv_capacity` forces smaller buffers (test hook). `zerv-model-capture` and
  `tools/verify_model.py --kv-capacity-mib` expose it.
- New one-cache limit: 491,520 tokens. The activation arena (prefill scores) and free
  VRAM bind first.
- The server now explains `InvalidContext` (multiple of 32) and `ContextTooLarge`.

## Verification (all executed)

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `verify_model.py` default oracles, modes 0 and 512, default buffers ([report](data/2026-09-24-kv-buffers/verify-default.json)) | pass (same worst/bound ratios as before) |
| same, forced 24 MiB KV buffers: **6 KV buffers**, 55–83 kernels ([report](data/2026-09-24-kv-buffers/verify-split-default.json)) | pass |
| long oracle (562 tokens), modes 0 and 512, default and forced split | pass |
| **bitwise**: `logits.bin` and `tensors.bin` of every case and mode against the pre-change tool (`baseline-capture`, sha `91e8be93…`) on the same inputs, and default against the 6-buffer split | **identical, 24 of 24 files** |
| `zig build test` (Debug and ReleaseFast) 83/83; Python unittest; `zig fmt --check` | pass |

Scripts: [gate.sh](data/2026-09-24-kv-buffers/gate.sh) (interrupted after three runs by
a session interruption), [gate2.sh](data/2026-09-24-kv-buffers/gate2.sh) (the rerun of the
rest).

## Beyond the old cap (end to end)

The server was run with `--context 38400 --spec-draft 3 --prefix-cache-slots 2`: it needed
23,440 MiB of 23,789 MiB free, and the card showed 24,061 of 24,560 MiB in use. The prompt
was 37,827 tokens: a "needle" sentence, then 100,000 characters of this repository's docs,
then a question about the needle ([manifest](data/2026-09-24-kv-buffers/needle-manifest.json),
